extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, teachers of literature, serious writers, and educated readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging prose, poetry, and criticism (style, tone, intellectual balance, metrical vehicles, and the influence of cultural centres/academies). Focuses on what makes criticism and poetry urbane, persuasive, and of lasting value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provinciality (negative quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'note of provinciality' in a writer or critic: provincial by matter even if not by style; lack of a central, widely-tested standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by exaggerating the value of one's ideas, giving one idea too much prominence at the expense of others, ordering ideas amiss, being hurried away by fancies, and liking/disliking too passionately or exclusively (e.g., 'admiration weeps hysterical tears, and its disapprobation foams at the mouth'). Avoid letting local or limited perspective harden into fixed crotchets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urbanity of style (civility and measured banter)
rubrics_metrics.description: An urbane critical style aims at a spiritual and intellectual effect; it combines banter with politeness and felicity rather than rancour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urbanity persuades rather than attacks; banter should not be disjoined from politeness. Cultivate temperance, measure, and a tone that aims to satisfy reason and taste rather than to inflame the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance — mental equilibrium and proportion — is essential: without it criticism becomes extravagant or violent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good critics and writers maintain balance so as not to lose 'measure' or 'centrality.' Lack of balance produces freaks, violences, or overemphasis on trivial points; strive for measured judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness, measure, and centrality in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'fitness, the measure, the centrality' are described as 'the soul of all good criticism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should aim for fitness (appropriate emphasis), measure (proportion), and centrality (focus on what matters). These qualities distinguish persuasive, lasting criticism from mere rant or extravagance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion through proof and preparation (not violence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true intellectual mode is persuasion — the instilment of conviction — not astonishing or contradicting without proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rhetorical violence: do not contradict familiar notions without preparation or evidence. Use reasoned argument, demonstration, and gradual instillation of conviction rather than surprise, shock, or mere assertion ('it simply astounds and irritates the hearer').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving one idea undue prominence; order ideas well
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not elevate a single idea excessively or disorder your ideas; avoid making one notion swallow others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For want of a high standard, provincial critics 'give one idea too much prominence at the expense of others' — guard against this by ordering ideas properly, preserving distinctions and shades of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint, checks, and accountability (value of centres/academies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of influential centres or academies exerts a restraining, corrective effect: they raise standards, create cultivated opinion, and compel temperate expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being 'speaking before competent judges' enforces sobriety and prevents extravagance. Where such centres are absent, critics may rely on 'the strength of his lungs' and be tempted to outrage; seek peer correction and cultivated standards to check excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid newspaper-style short, highly-charged writing in serious criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper prose often exemplifies provincial defects: party spirit, avoidance of shades and distinctions, short highly-charged 'heavy-shotted' articles aiming at blood and senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious criticism should not adopt the newspaper's hard-hitting, absolutist tone; prefer subtlety, distinctions, and intellectual aims over sensational or partisan effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style types and their evaluative features (Attic / Asiatic / Corinthian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Styles are typified: Attic (warm glow, blithe movement, soft pliancy, sureness), Asiatic (over-heavy richness, encumbered gait), Corinthian (glitter without warmth, rapidity without ease, effectiveness without charm; 'no soul').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an author's style by these qualities: aspire toward Attic virtues of lightness, naturalness, and grace; beware Corinthian glitter that aims only at effect and triumph and lacks soul and simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of poetic vehicle / metre
rubrics_metrics.description: The established metrical vehicle must be adequate to convey high poetic matters; inadequacy of metre disadvantages poets (e.g., the French alexandrine and the English ten-syllable couplet are said to be inadequate for continuous high poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the language's established metre or vehicle suits the poet's purpose. Poets using inadequate vehicles are handicapped compared to those with more adequate forms (blank verse, hexameter, iambics). Consider whether prose might be a better vehicle for certain poetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretative power of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: One of poetry's highest powers is interpretative power: to awaken in us a wonderfully full, new, and intimate sense of objects and our relation to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetry by whether it awakens that intimate sense (bringing the object's secret into sympathetic knowledge), whether it moves the whole person rather than appealing to limited faculties as science does. This power is rare and precious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius versus technical precision (trade-offs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer may have genius and powerful ideas but lack the best style; conversely, one with precision of style but not genius may lack striking ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the trade-off and value both qualities; cultivate widening culture and checks to temper shortcomings. Strive to combine powerful ideas with adequate stylistic control when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and editorial tact (anthology/collection decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial arrangement (e.g., Palgrave's Golden Treasury) can show delicate feeling and critical tact; the juxtaposition of pieces can be a mark of critical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editors/critics for their sense of order and proportion in arranging material; good arrangement can reveal critical delicacy and improve reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'freaks' and gratuitous disparagements
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical notes that contradict common views without preparation or that indulge in gratuitous disparagement are described as 'freaks' or 'violences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't express strong judgments without proof or measured argument. Even if an unconventional view is right, express it with preparation and reason; otherwise it becomes mere violence and undermines fitness and centrality.
